issues.legal_issue: Conviction and imprisonment do not extinguish all fundamental rights, although incarceration necessarily limits freedoms incompatible with confinement.
material_facts: The petitioners were serving prison sentences, and some were also held as under-trial prisoners.
They claimed that measures within and around the prison infringed their fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: Prisoners retain fundamental rights, including the right to life and personal liberty, except to the extent particular rights are necessarily limited by lawful incarceration.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 21 and 13 of the Constitution. It relied on State of Maharashtra v. Prabhakar Pandurang Sanzgiri, which held that detention does not remove every aspect of personal liberty, and on Kharak Singh v. State of U.P., which approved the understanding in Munn v. Illinois that life means more than mere animal existence. Conviction necessarily curtails freedoms such as movement throughout India and practising a profession, but does not extinguish all fundamental rights.

predicates.constitutional_writ_by_prisoner: A prisoner brings a constitutional writ proceeding asserting rights during incarceration.
predicates.prisoner_claims_fundamental_rights: The prisoner asserts that conduct during incarceration affects fundamental rights.
predicates.incarceration_limits_some_freedoms: The prisoner is confined in a way that necessarily prevents the exercise of some freedoms.

issues.definition: When a prisoner brings a constitutional writ asserting fundamental rights, and confinement necessarily limits some freedoms, the prisoner retains other fundamental rights.

issues.legal_issue: Posting police guards outside a prison does not infringe prisoners’ fundamental rights when the guards cannot access the prison and their presence does not interfere with prisoners’ liberty or lawful activities.
material_facts: The ordinary prison watch and ward staff were considered inadequate after a large number of prisoners were housed there.
Prisoners had escaped previously, prompting additional security measures.
Police guards occupied land immediately outside the prison, which was enclosed by high walls.
The guards were not shown to have access to the prison or to interfere with the prisoners’ personal liberty or lawful activities.
issues.conclusion: The posting of the guards did not deprive the petitioners of any fundamental right, and the prisoners were not entitled to have the guards removed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 21 and 13 of the Constitution and section 3(1) of the Prisons Act, 1894, which includes appurtenant land within the definition of a prison. It recognized that police intrusion into prisons is generally to be deprecated, particularly in relation to under-trial prisoners, but held that the guards’ presence nearby was not an infringement where they had no access to the prison and caused no interference with liberty or lawful activities.

predicates.constitutional_writ_by_prisoner: A prisoner challenges a prison-related measure in a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.outside_guards_posted_for_prison_securit: Authorities post guards outside a prison to prevent escapes or address inadequate internal security.
predicates.guards_cannot_access_prison: The guards are outside the enclosed prison and are not shown to have access to its interior.
predicates.guards_do_not_interfere_with_prisoners: The guards’ presence does not interfere with prisoners’ personal liberty or lawful activities.

issues.definition: When guards are posted outside a prison for security, cannot access it, and do not interfere with prisoners, their presence does not infringe prisoners’ fundamental rights.

issues.legal_issue: Allegations of inhuman prison treatment do not establish a violation of the right to life or personal liberty when the evidence does not satisfactorily prove the alleged treatment.
material_facts: The petitioners alleged segregation and inhuman treatment in prison.
The jail authorities described the conditions and facilities as adequate, while the petitioners disputed that account.
The Court was not satisfied that the allegations of inhuman treatment were proved, although it did not accept the authorities’ account uncritically.
issues.conclusion: The alleged treatment was not shown to violate the petitioners’ right to life or personal liberty; the Court nevertheless observed that barbarous treatment of prisoners offends the Constitution’s letter and spirit and that humane prison conditions deserve attention.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 21 of the Constitution. It observed that prisoners may be subjected to subtle forms of punishment and that barbarous treatment is inconsistent with the Constitution. It also referred to Article 42 as a directive principle that could benevolently be extended to living conditions in jails, while holding that the particular allegations were not established by satisfactory proof.

predicates.constitutional_writ_by_prisoner: A prisoner challenges prison conditions in a constitutional writ proceeding.
predicates.prisoner_alleges_inhuman_treatment: The prisoner alleges that authorities subjected prisoners to inhuman treatment.
predicates.not_sufficient_evidence_of_alleged_treat: The evidence in the proceeding does not satisfactorily establish the alleged treatment.

issues.definition: When a prisoner alleges inhuman treatment in a constitutional writ proceeding but the evidence does not satisfactorily establish it, a fundamental-rights violation is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A live-wire deterrent on prison walls does not infringe a prisoner’s fundamental rights when it cannot be contacted during ordinary lawful activities and can be encountered only while attempting to escape lawful custody.
material_facts: A high-voltage wire was installed above the prison wall on non-conductors, separated from the wall, and regularly inspected.
Prisoners were warned that the wire was present, and a barbed-wire fence also protected the wall.
The prison wall was separated from the prisoners’ cells, and the evidence showed no possibility of contact during ordinary daily activities or by a person performing lawful functions.
A prisoner could encounter the wire only by attempting to escape from lawful custody.
issues.conclusion: The live-wire mechanism did not interfere with the petitioners’ fundamental freedoms, so they were not entitled to have it dismantled.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Articles 21 and 13(3)(a) of the Constitution. It held that an administrative instruction is not law or procedure established by law, so a measure that infringes a fundamental right must be justified by law. But the wire did not infringe the petitioners’ rights because they had no fundamental freedom to escape lawful custody and could encounter it only while attempting escape. The Court held that section 46(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, was not contravened and that section 66 of that Code, concerning pursuit and retaking after escape, did not make the device unconstitutional; it also considered the submission concerning section 224 of the Penal Code.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_by_prisoner and live_wire_installed_as_escape_deterrent and wire_cannot_be_contacted_during_lawful_daily_activities and wire_contact_requires_escape_attempt
